56      The Savoy Male and Female College

in the collegiate department are at graduation hardly able to enter upon the sophomore or second year work of the better Northern colleges.

The Savoy College Curriculum versus the Typical Curriculum.—As Savoy College's most abbreviated course, that leading to the diploma without a degree, required four years of work beyond an eight-year preparatory base, it appears that this coverage would in quantity of work meet the lower mark derived by President Thomas and the Commissioner of Education; and it advances actually to the sophomore class in better eastern universities. Beyond this minimum certificate level, the College's Freshman, Sophomore, Junior, Senior course gives us an additional four-year or two of intensive work, and the ambitious schedule of the A.B. degree would require, or mark even more—perhaps two years, by a count of courses.

    And perhaps the quantity and subject matter covered is more significant than a measure of work in student years. With President Halsell offering both a college preparatory and college course as a basis of comparison, it is seen that in the better schools the student would expect coverage in Latin, Greek, and mathematics (Caesar, The American Score): three books of the Anabasis, one-and-a-half books of the Iliad, and arithmetic to quadratics—as the prescribed Freshman work for the Savoy College A.B., was in the Primary and Preparatory departments. With this course count, then, Savoy College would appear to fall in the class of the "weaker" colleges, which had to review the preparatory subjects in the first year of the college course.

    It is significant and the fact that each pupil was personally identified by his name rather than number or division) and each student was the assigned to a teacher, who in was expected to remain there all during the school hours doing reciting recitations from all the various subjects, primarily to the recitation benches of the various professors according to schedule, and to other parts of the buildings in many cases, from their seats in the room. Pupils in the lower-class and from their seats there recited all their lessons—all had been in charge of class room.
